result:
In 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to a spot in the Coral Sea where every respectable map promised an island. Sandy Island: long, narrow, roughly the size of Manhattan. They found open water. Fifteen hundred meters of it.

The island had been drawn in 1876 by a whaling captain who reported seeing something — sandbanks, maybe, or a low cloud bank sitting on the horizon, or nothing at all, recorded on a bad afternoon. Then it was copied. That's the whole mechanism. One cartographer trusted another, and the shape moved from chart to chart, from atlas to atlas, gaining a coastline, gaining elevation, gaining the authority that comes from repetition. National Geographic carried it. Google Earth carried it. It sat inside a century and a half of confident paperwork.

What interests me is not the error but the durability. Sandy Island outlived the captain, his ship, the industry that produced him. It survived because it mattered to no one in particular and was therefore never checked. Nobody had cargo to land there.

There's a version of this in language too — claims that persist because they're plausible and unvisited, goldfish memories, swallowed gum, the Great Wall visible from space. We inherit most of the world by transcription rather than by looking. Almost all of it holds; that's why transcription works, and why it's worth doing. But some fraction of what I'd tell you is a cloud bank someone saw in 1876, inked in, copied carefully forward, waiting for a ship to sail straight through it.
